difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (policy → reduced emissions → improved air quality outcome). The weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion by introducing an alternative causal factor driving the observed outcome. Distractors include one strengthener, one out-of-scope environmental fact, and one choice that attacks a peripheral premise without touching the conclusion.
stimulus: A regional environmental authority enacted strict vehicle-emission standards four years ago. Since then, the average concentration of ground-level ozone in the region has declined by 22 percent. The authority's director concluded that the emission standards were responsible for the improvement in air quality.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the same four-year period, a major industrial plant in the region—responsible for a substantial portion of local ozone precursor emissions—permanently shut down its operations one year before the emission standards took effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neighboring regions that did not adopt similar emission standards experienced no significant change in ground-level ozone concentrations over the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ground-level ozone is known to cause respiratory problems in people with pre-existing lung conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vehicle-emission standards were more stringent than those required by national environmental law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some vehicle owners in the region delayed compliance with the new emission standards by obtaining temporary exemptions.

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that the emission standards caused the 22% decline in ozone. Choice A introduces an alternative cause—the shutdown of a major industrial polluter—that preceded the standards' implementation and could independently explain the ozone reduction, thereby undermining the director's causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces a competing cause (industrial plant closure) that predates and could fully account for the observed improvement, severing the claimed link between the emission standards and the air-quality outcome.
explanations.B: This is a strengthener, not a weakener. The absence of improvement in regions without the standards supports the conclusion that the standards drove the change; it is the opposite-answer trap.
explanations.C: Out-of-scope. The health effects of ground-level ozone are irrelevant to whether the emission standards caused its decline.
explanations.D: Strengthener or irrelevant. The stringency of the standards, if anything, bolsters the claim they were effective; it does not weaken the causal conclusion.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Some delayed compliance weakens implementation fidelity only marginally and doesn't undermine the overall causal conclusion—it leaves open that sufficient compliance still drove the decline.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument with a two-step inferential move: historical success of a technology → adoption of that technology in a new context → predicted economic benefit. The correct weakener attacks the move from evidence to conclusion by exposing a disanalogy between the historical case and the new context. Distractors include a strengthener and an accurate-but-irrelevant economic fact.
stimulus: A technology consulting firm recently advised a mid-sized retail bank to adopt an AI-driven loan-underwriting system. The firm pointed to the fact that three large investment banks that implemented the same system last year reported a 30 percent reduction in loan-default rates. The consulting firm concluded that the retail bank would also experience a significant reduction in loan defaults if it adopted the system.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the consulting firm's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The AI-driven underwriting system was originally designed to evaluate the creditworthiness of large corporate borrowers, and its predictive models have not been validated for the consumer and small-business lending that constitutes the retail bank's entire portfolio.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The three investment banks that adopted the system are headquartered in the same financial district and share several major institutional clients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loan-default rates at large investment banks tend to fluctuate more sharply than those at retail banks because of differences in loan size and duration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The retail bank's current loan-underwriting process relies on a combination of human judgment and rule-based software that was last updated five years ago.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several other AI-driven financial software products have successfully reduced administrative costs for retail banks in markets similar to this one.

explanations.correct: The firm's conclusion rests on an analogy: because the system worked for large investment banks, it will work for the retail bank. Choice A exposes a critical disanalogy—the system was built and validated only for large corporate borrowers, not for the consumer and small-business lending that the retail bank actually does. This directly undercuts the analogical inference.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a fundamental disanalogy between the cases on which the prediction is based and the target case, severing the analogical bridge the consulting firm's argument requires.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. The shared clients and location of the investment banks don't bear on whether the system will transfer effectively to a retail-lending context; this is a shift-in-subject trap.
explanations.C: Too narrow / inaccurate target. This describes a general difference in volatility between the two types of banks but doesn't explain why the system itself would fail in the retail context; it could even be read as supporting the conclusion (retail defaults are more predictable).
explanations.D: Strengthener or irrelevant. The outdated state of the retail bank's current system might actually support the consulting firm's recommendation; it doesn't weaken the prediction.
explanations.E: Strengthener. Evidence that AI-driven systems benefit retail banks supports, rather than undermines, the consulting firm's conclusion.

difficultyReason: Causal argument in a medical/policy context where the conclusion generalizes from a study's correlation to a population-level recommendation. The correct weakener introduces a confounding variable that explains the correlation without supporting the causal claim. One distractor strengthens by ruling out a rival explanation; another is out-of-scope.
stimulus: Researchers studying a large urban hospital found that patients who were visited by a hospital social worker within 24 hours of admission had significantly shorter average hospital stays than patients who were not visited. The researchers concluded that early social-worker visits reduce the length of hospital stays and recommended that all hospitals implement mandatory early social-worker rounds.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the researchers' argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Social workers at the hospital were assigned to visit patients whose medical charts indicated a straightforward, uncomplicated recovery prognosis, while patients with more complex conditions were referred to specialist case managers instead.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hospitals that have implemented mandatory social-worker rounds have reported improvements in patient satisfaction scores independent of changes in length of stay.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hospital in the study had a higher ratio of social workers to patients than most other urban hospitals in the country.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several studies conducted at rural hospitals have found no statistically significant relationship between social-worker visits and length of stay.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Early social-worker visits help patients arrange post-discharge care, which is one mechanism by which hospital stays could plausibly be shortened.

explanations.correct: The researchers infer that early social-worker visits cause shorter stays. Choice A reveals that social workers were selectively assigned to patients already expected to recover quickly. This means the correlation could reflect patient-complexity selection bias rather than any causal effect of the visits—patients with shorter stays were predisposed to shorter stays regardless of the visits.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a confounding variable (case complexity / recovery prognosis) that accounts for the correlation between early social-worker visits and shorter stays without requiring any causal role for the visits, directly undermining the causal conclusion.
explanations.B: Out-of-scope. Patient satisfaction is a separate outcome; this choice neither supports nor undermines the claim that visits reduce length of stay, making it an accurate-but-irrelevant trap.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. The staff ratio might explain why the hospital could conduct early visits but says nothing about whether those visits actually caused shorter stays; this is a shift-in-subject trap.
explanations.D: Too narrow / potential strengthener of doubt, but misapplied. The absence of an effect at rural hospitals introduces a different population; it doesn't explain away the urban hospital's correlation and leaves the researchers' finding unexplained. A careful reader may think this weakens, but it doesn't attack the causal inference from the study's own data.
explanations.E: Strengthener. Providing a plausible causal mechanism by which visits could shorten stays bolsters the researchers' causal conclusion rather than weakening it; this is the opposite-answer trap.
